d.title: Stability is a guarantee, which is what makes a multi-pass sort work
d.caption: **Timsort is stable: elements comparing equal keep their original relative order** — and that is a documented guarantee rather than an observation, which is what lets you **sort by several keys in separate passes, least significant first.** The output shows it: `beth` and `carol` both have 50.0 and stay in input order. **`key=` is called once per element**, so an expensive key is cheap here and ruinous in a comparison function — and **`operator.itemgetter("total")` is faster than the equivalent lambda.**

d.title: The usual explanation is true and pedagogically misleading
d.caption: ***A tuple is an immutable list* is technically correct and teaches the wrong instinct.** The distinction experienced engineers actually use is **what the positions mean** — and there is a one-line test: **if you would be comfortable appending an element, it is a list; if appending would make no sense because the fields are positional, it is a tuple.** It also explains a syntax that otherwise looks strange: **`return x, y` returns a tuple, and `for k, v in d.items()` unpacks one.**

columns.title: List
items: many items of the SAME kind
you iterate over all of them

columns.title: Tuple
items: a few fields of DIFFERENT kinds
position 0 is always the same field
length is fixed by the data's structure
you unpack it into named variables

d.title: It exists because it is hashable, and that is a narrower reason than it looks
d.caption: **A `frozenset` is an immutable set, and because it cannot change it is hashable — which means it can be a dictionary key or an element of another set.** That is the whole reason it exists. The narrowness is worth stating: **if you only need “this set should not be modified”, a plain `set` and a convention costs nothing** — the type earns its place only when something downstream requires hashability, such as **keying a cache on a set of permissions, or deduplicating sets of tags.**

d.title: A language guarantee since 3.7, not a CPython detail
d.caption: **Dicts preserve insertion order — an implementation detail in CPython 3.6 and a language guarantee in 3.7 — so it is safe to rely on across implementations, not merely in CPython.** The third line is the part worth noticing: **re-assigning an existing key keeps its original position, while deleting and re-inserting moves it to the end.** Which means **an in-place update preserves order and a delete-then-set does not**, and the two look equivalent in a diff.

d.title: A view is a live window, and the key view does set algebra
d.caption: **`d.keys()`, `d.values()` and `d.items()` return views — live windows onto the dict rather than copies — so they reflect later changes and cost nothing to create.** The second property is the one people miss: **the key and item views support set operations directly**, so `a.keys() - b.keys()` gives the keys only `a` has, with no intermediate sets built. **Being live is also the trap: mutating the dict while iterating a view raises `RuntimeError`**, which is why you wrap it in `list()` to iterate and delete.

state: a live view, not a copy

d.title: Later keys win, and the merge is one level deep
d.caption: **`{**defaults, **overrides}` resolves a duplicate key in favour of the later mapping** — which is what makes the layered-configuration idiom work at all. The limit is the one 2.9 §04 returns to: **the merge is shallow, so a nested dict in `overrides` replaces the whole nested dict in `defaults` rather than merging into it.** For a flat config that is exactly right; for `{'db': {'host': ..., 'port': ...}}` **overriding only the host silently drops the port.**

d.title: Slice assignment edits the object, so every alias sees it
d.caption: **A slice on the left of an assignment replaces that region in place — the list object stays the same, so every name bound to it sees the change.** Which is the difference from `lst = [...]`, and the reason the aliasing lesson matters here. The length changes are the part that surprises: **assigning three items into a one-item slice grows the list**, and **assigning an empty list into a slice deletes that region** — so `lst[1:3] = []` is a deletion written as an assignment.

d.title: Four of these five are O(n) and copy pointers only
d.caption: The column that matters is the third: **a list or dict copy is `O(n)` and copies *pointers*, so the nested objects are shared** — which is why a shallow copy of a list of dicts gives you a new list whose dicts are the originals. **`copy.deepcopy` is the only one that follows the whole graph, tracking cycles, and it is `O(total graph)`** rather than `O(n)`. And the row that is free: **`tuple(t)` on a tuple returns the same object, because it cannot change.**

steps.code: tuple(t) where t is a tuple

d.title: Concurrency removes the accident of timing that was hiding the flaw
d.caption: **Shared mutable state is a bug in a single-threaded program too — it is just harder to observe, because nothing else runs between your read and your write.** The output makes it concrete: two call sites, **`{'limit': 50}` twice**, one object. So **concurrency does not introduce the flaw; it removes the accident of timing that was hiding it** — which is why “it only breaks under load” is a statement about observability rather than about cause, and why the fix is the same in both cases.

d.title: Three dispatch shapes, and the third one moves the branch into the data
d.caption: **A chain of `elif` comparing the same variable against constants is a lookup written as control flow — past three or four branches a dict usually reads better and is easier to extend.** The three forms differ in what the values are: **a constant per key, a function per key when each branch does work, or a method on the object itself when the branch genuinely belongs to the data.** The last is the one that scales, **because adding a case means adding a class rather than editing a dispatcher.**

state: the branch belongs to the data

d.title: One conditional reads well, three nested ones do not
d.caption: **Inside a comprehension, an f-string or an argument list a statement is not allowed — the conditional expression is the only option, and that is what it is for rather than saving a line.** The degradation is quick: **two branches is still readable, three is already hard, and four wraps across lines and should be a table.** Which is what the last row is: **`GRADES[bisect_right(CUTOFFS, score)]` replaces the whole chain with sorted data and one lookup.**

steps.code: 'high' if s > 90 else 'mid' if s > 50 else 'low'

d.title: A sequence of items, or a condition that changes
d.caption: **`for` is for consuming a sequence of items — known in advance or produced by something — and that is the overwhelming majority of loops.** `while` is for **repeating until a condition changes where there is no natural sequence: polling, retrying, a REPL, consuming a queue that refills.** Which is a useful test to apply in review: **a `while` loop with a counter you increment yourself is almost always a `for` loop over a range**, and the manual counter is where the off-by-one lives.

d.title: Holding the data twice is a normal trade, and the discipline is the risk
d.caption: **Choosing a container is not always exclusive. When two access patterns both matter, holding the data twice is a normal engineering trade — you are spending memory to remove an order of complexity.** Here a list keeps order and a set answers membership in `O(1)`. **The cost is roughly double the memory and the discipline of keeping the two views consistent — and that discipline is the real risk**, which is why the synchronisation belongs **inside one small class rather than scattered across callers.**

nodes.label: Hold both
nodes.sub: memory for an order of complexity

nodes.label: So confine it to one small class

d.title: One nested order becomes two flat rows, and an empty dict survives flattening
d.caption: **Reshaping nested data into flat rows is the commonest transformation there is — one order with two line items becomes two rows, each carrying the order and customer fields repeated.** Which is the shape every analytics tool wants and no API returns. The flattening row is the edge case worth having a decision about: **`{'e': {}}` flattens to `{'e': {}}` rather than disappearing**, because there is no leaf inside it — so **an empty branch is either preserved as a value or lost, and the recursion has to choose.**

d.title: `key=` changes what is compared, not what is returned
d.caption: **`max(orders, key=...)` returns the order, not the total** — which is the distinction that makes these three built-ins replace a best-so-far loop rather than just a comparison. So `max` with a key gives you the whole record to work with, and if you wanted the number you ask for it afterwards. Two details worth carrying: **`min`/`max` raise on an empty iterable unless you pass `default=`**, and **`sorted` returns a new list and is stable**, so 2.1's multi-pass technique applies here too.

d.title: It stopped at 2, which is the whole reason to keep it a generator
d.caption: **`any` and `all` short-circuit — the trace prints `checking 0`, `checking 1`, `checking 2` and then stops, because the third element satisfied it.** Which is why the argument should be a generator expression and not a list comprehension: **`any([f(x) for x in xs])` evaluates `f` for every element before `any` sees any of them, so the short-circuit is thrown away.** Dropping two brackets changes the cost from `O(n)` to `O(position of the first match)`.

d.title: Two different positions for a condition, doing two different jobs
d.caption: **A condition at the end filters — fewer elements come out. A conditional expression at the front transforms — the same number of elements come out, mapped.** Which is why the two can be combined and are not alternatives: `[f(x) if c(x) else g(x) for x in xs if keep(x)]` filters first and then maps what survives. The third row is the readability limit: **once both are present and either expression is non-trivial, a named function or a loop is the clearer version.**

steps.code: [x for x in xs if x % 2]
['+' if x > 0 else '-' for x in xs]

d.title: Dropping two brackets took 8,448,728 bytes to 200
d.caption: **A list comprehension over a million items allocates 8,448,728 bytes; the generator expression is 200 bytes, because it holds a recipe rather than a result** — a 42,000× difference, and the sum over it is identical. So the rule is about what happens next: **use a generator when you are feeding `sum`, `any`, `max` or a `for` loop, and a list when you need to index it, measure its length, or iterate it more than once.** The last point is the trap: **a generator is consumed once, and the second pass sees nothing.**

d.title: The comprehension variable does not leak, and that is a Python 3 change
d.caption: **A comprehension has its own scope, so the loop variable does not leak into the enclosing function — the outer `x` prints `unchanged`.** This was not true in Python 2, which is why older code sometimes relies on the leak. The second row is the part that still catches people: **the iterable of the outermost `for` is evaluated in the enclosing scope, while everything else is evaluated inside** — which is why a comprehension at class level can see the class's names in that first iterable and nowhere else.

state: only that iterable sees class names
